4	LLM-based automated program repair systems increasingly rely on test-time compute scaling: generating $K$ candidate patches and selecting the best via a verifier~\cite{snell2024scaling}. Full execution verification is reliable but expensive (\$1--3 per candidate at repository scale\footnote{Based on per-instance costs reported by \citet{yang2024sweagent} and \citet{xia2024agentless}.}), driving demand for execution-free alternatives. Three distinct formulations have emerged for this task: \textbf{generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution} predicts execution output strings per test; \textbf{trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{shum2025swerm} predicts a binary patch verdict without per-test decomposition; and \textbf{per-test classification}~\cite{ni2023lever,chen2023codet} predicts a pass/fail token per test. Each makes different tradeoffs between diagnostic granularity, output complexity, and inference cost.
5	
6	Despite active development along each axis, no prior work provides a systematic comparison holding model capacity, training data, and compute constant. Practitioners choosing a formulation for their verification pipeline must rely on results from different models, different datasets, and different evaluation protocols. Whether one formulation is uniformly preferable, or whether the choice depends on properties of the code being verified, remains an open empirical question. A related question is whether formulation choice matters at all relative to more basic decisions: at what complexity level does fine-tuning become necessary, and does formulation selection add value beyond what fine-tuning alone provides?

2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	Let $p$ denote a candidate patch and $T = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ its test suite, where each $t_i$ has label $y_i \in \{\text{\textsc{Pass}}, \text{\textsc{Fail}}\}$ from execution. Tests decompose into \emph{fail-to-pass} ($T_{\text{f2p}}$) and \emph{pass-to-pass} ($T_{\text{p2p}}$) subsets; a patch is correct iff $\forall\, t_i{:}\ y_i = \text{\textsc{Pass}}$. We compare three formulations for predicting correctness without execution.
5	
6	\subsection{Verification Formulations}
7	\label{sec:formulations}
8	
9	Let $c_p$ denote the code context (unified diff) of patch $p$.
10	
11	\paragraph{\cls{} (per-test classification).} $f(c_p, t_i) \rightarrow \hat{y}_i \in \{\text{\textsc{Pass}}, \text{\textsc{Fail}}\}$ predicts a single binary token per test (cross-entropy loss). Patch verdict: $\hat{y}_p = \bigwedge_{i} [\hat{y}_i = \text{\textsc{Pass}}]$. Output cost: one token per test.
12	
13	\paragraph{\cwm{} (output generation).} $g(c_p, t_i) \rightarrow \hat{o}_i \in \Sigma^*$ generates the execution output string (language modeling loss). Verdict by exact match: $\hat{y}_i = \text{\textsc{Pass}}$ iff $\hat{o}_i = o_i^*$.\footnote{Exact string matching is conservative, consistent with \citet{meta2025cwm}. Semantic equivalences are not counted.} When the generated output is unparseable (i.e., does not conform to the expected structured format), the prediction defaults to the majority class verdict. Output cost: $\sum_i |\hat{o}_i|$ tokens.
14	
15	\paragraph{\traj{} (trajectory-level).} $h(c_p, T) \rightarrow \hat{y}_p \in \{\text{\textsc{Resolved}}, \text{\textsc{Unresolved}}\}$ predicts a single patch verdict from all tests and provides no per-test signal. \traj{} serves as a granularity control: \cls{}--\traj{} differences isolate the value of per-test decomposition independent of the classification formulation itself.

\paragraph{Default assignment artifact.} The apparent \cwm{} ``improvement'' from 4B (58.04\%) to 8B (65.17\%) is an artifact: as unparseable rate increases from 53.7\% to 73.8\%, more predictions default to the majority class (pass, 72.96\%), inflating accuracy. Parseable-only accuracy \emph{decreases} from 42.88\% (4B) to 38.52\% (8B). Gold mutation (unmodified code) parse rate collapses from 43.5\% to 23.9\%; even the simplest generation target exhibits a fundamental bottleneck (Appendix~\ref{app:repo_mutation}). This alignment is not coincidental: unparseable instances have significantly higher pass rates than parseable ones (74.6\% vs.\ 68.3\%, $\chi^2$ $p = 5.9 \times 10^{-10}$), and are systematically easier for \cls{} models (\cls{} accuracy 86.4\% vs.\ 79.1\%, $p = 3.3 \times 10^{-18}$). \cwm{}'s parsing failures concentrate on simpler, pass-heavy instances, inflating reported accuracy through default assignment (cross-model Jaccard overlap 0.46 confirms this is instance-driven; Appendix~\ref{app:parseable_bias}). The directional impact is unambiguous: correcting for this artifact would \emph{widen} the \cls{}--\cwm{} gap beyond the 19--26\pp{} reported in Table~\ref{tab:repo_level}.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.} Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{willard2023outlines} could eliminate format compliance failures, but parseable-only accuracy (42.88\% at 4B, 38.52\% at 8B) is well below majority baseline even among well-formed outputs. The fundamental bottleneck is output space complexity, not format compliance. Resolving format failures would expose the underlying semantic prediction gap rather than close the accuracy divide.

\paragraph{Training and evaluation sensitivity.} No \cwm{} overtraining is observed: epoch 2 and 3 final checkpoints achieve comparable running accuracy (${\sim}$65\%, $<$2\pp{} difference) at matched settings. Evaluation protocol introduces ${\sim}$9\pp{} variation for the same checkpoint (seq2048: ${\sim}$65\% vs.\ seq4096: ${\sim}$56\%), driven by the unparseable rate $\to$ majority-class default chain. Practitioners must standardize evaluation sequence length; \cls{} is invariant to this parameter. Table~\ref{tab:repo_level} \cwm{} values use different eval lengths across models (Qwen3: 8192, DeepSeek: 4096); the qualitative conclusion (format collapse, below-majority accuracy) holds at all tested lengths, but precise cross-model \cwm{} numbers are not directly comparable.

\subsection{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

We identify five potential confounds and assess their impact on our conclusions.

\paragraph{Checkpoint selection.} Val-based selection is unavailable for runs with NaN validation loss (all \cwm{} repo-level runs, DeepSeek \cls{} s123), which default to the final epoch checkpoint. The Qwen3-8B \traj{} comparison (epoch 2: 72.92\% vs.\ epoch 3: 70.83\%) illustrates that a single epoch difference can shift accuracy by ${\sim}$2\pp{}. Val-selected and final-epoch checkpoints are not directly comparable. The magnitude of this confound is bounded by the ${\leq}$2\pp{} epoch-to-epoch variation observed within each formulation.

\paragraph{Evaluation sequence length.} \cwm{} accuracy varies by ${\sim}$9\pp{} across evaluation sequence lengths for the same checkpoint (seq2048: ${\sim}$65\% vs.\ seq4096: ${\sim}$56\%), driven by unparseable-rate differences that propagate through majority-class default assignment. \cls{} is invariant to this parameter. Cross-model \cwm{} comparisons use different eval lengths (Qwen3: 8192, DeepSeek: 4096) and are not directly comparable in absolute terms. A matched-sequence evaluation shows ${\sim}$1.5\pp{} difference for \cls{} (Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}), insufficient to explain the 19--26\pp{} gap.

\paragraph{Preprocessing.} DeepSeek \cls{} accuracy ranges from 82.61\% (s42, drop preprocessing) to 74.93\% (s123, truncate preprocessing), a 7.68\pp{} spread that conflates preprocessing strategy, checkpoint selection method, and seed. The two strategies produce different effective training sets (67,343 vs.\ 70,748 samples) and different checkpoint selection regimes. The qualitative ranking \cls{} $>$ \cwm{} holds under both strategies (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{\traj{} training regime.} \traj{} uses a different training configuration: smaller training set (${\sim}$400 repo-level variants vs.\ ${\sim}$70K per-test instances), higher learning rate ($2{\times}10^{-4}$ vs.\ $5{\times}10^{-5}$), and variant-level labels. This asymmetry is inherent to the formulation (trajectory-level labels are only available at variant granularity), but precludes training-data-controlled comparison at repo level. The downsample ablation confirms the \cls{} formulation advantage persists at matched data volume (80.74\% vs.\ 72.92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:downsample}).

\paragraph{\cwm{} scale and pretraining.} Our \cwm{} baseline uses 4--8B LoRA fine-tuning without execution trace pretraining. The original Code World Model~\cite{meta2025cwm} uses 32B parameters with mid-training on execution traces, a fundamentally different training regime. At larger scale or with execution-trace pretraining, the generation bottleneck observed here may diminish: larger models produce more coherent long-form outputs, and execution trace exposure may improve output format compliance. This is the primary limitation: all repo-level \cwm{} conclusions are conditional on the ${\leq}$8B LoRA regime.

Despite these confounds, the repo-level \cls{}--\cwm{} gap (19--26\pp{}) exceeds any individual confound's observed effect by an order of magnitude. Variant-level bootstrap analysis confirms the \cls{}--\cwm{} gap is well-powered (mean power $= 0.87$, 95\% CI lower bound: 10.42\pp{}; Appendix~\ref{app:power}). \cls{}--\traj{} comparisons are underpowered (mean power $= 0.08$) at $n{=}48$, consistent with our TOST equivalence finding: any true difference is too small to detect at this sample size. Holm-Bonferroni correction across the four primary comparisons ($k{=}4$) confirms both the \cls{}--\cwm{} gap (adjusted $p{=}0.012$) and function-level equivalence (adjusted $p{=}0.021$) survive; the repo-level \cwm{}--\traj{} comparison is directionally consistent but does not survive correction (adjusted $p{=}0.078$; Table~\ref{tab:holm}). The consistent direction across both model families and all tested configurations supports a formulation-level explanation, though definitive causal attribution requires future experiments addressing each confound individually.

\item \textbf{Formulation equivalence at low complexity.} On function-level benchmarks, \cls{}, \cwm{}, and \traj{} achieve near-equivalent accuracy across two model families (Qwen3-4B: 88.4/87.2/86.3\%, 5 seeds; DeepSeek-6.7B: 86.9/86.8\%, 2 seeds). This null result establishes that classification is not inherently easier than generation when execution outputs are short and structured.

\item \textbf{Evidence for complexity-dependent divergence with identified confounds.} At repository-level complexity under 4--8B LoRA fine-tuning, \cls{} achieves 19--26\pp{} higher accuracy than \cwm{} on Qwen3 (primary seed). Cross-model consistency check with DeepSeek-Coder is consistent with a formulation-driven explanation, though single-seed constraints and confounds (checkpoint selection, preprocessing, evaluation sequence length; \S\ref{sec:threats}) limit causal attribution. Both families show \cwm{} $>$ \cls{} degradation from function to repo level (Qwen3: ${\sim}$5/22\pp{}; DeepSeek: 4--12/25--30\pp{} for \cls{}/\cwm{}). The magnitude is model-contingent and seed-dependent: DeepSeek \cls{} degradation ranges from ${\sim}$4\pp{} (s42) to ${\sim}$12\pp{} (s123). Variant-level analysis reveals three distinct repo-level failure modes governed by formulation $\times$ checkpoint: format collapse (\cwm{}), decision collapse (\cls{}, checkpoint-dependent), and aggregation penalty (\cls{}); the same model family exhibits different modes depending on checkpoint selection (\S\ref{sec:repo}).

\item \textbf{Error complementarity.} At function level, \cls{} and \cwm{} exhibit opposite error patterns: \cls{} over-predicts passing (75.5\% false negatives), \cwm{} over-predicts failure (83.1\% false positives). An oracle ensemble achieves 90.63\% (+3.12\pp{}); whether this complementarity persists at repo level, where \cwm{} accuracy falls below majority baseline, remains open.

\item \textbf{Diagnostic granularity with configuration-dependent cost.} Per-test classification achieves equivalent variant-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST $p = 0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) at function level while identifying which specific tests fail. At repo level, aggregation penalty under the all-pass rule is configuration-dependent: DeepSeek s42 achieves 81.25\% variant-level (1.36\pp{} penalty), matching or exceeding trajectory-level (75.35\%), while other configurations pay 4--19\pp{} (\S\ref{sec:analysis}(k)). Classification yields 217$\times$ throughput over generation.

tool_args.old_string: \paragraph{(k) Aggregation penalty.} Per-test classification achieves high per-test accuracy at repo level, but variant-level accuracy under the all-pass rule drops substantially: Qwen3-8B 84.48--85.60\% per-test $\to$ 72.92--81.25\% variant-level (4--12\pp{} penalty, 2 seeds); Qwen3-4B 83.63\% $\to$ 64.58\% (19\pp{} penalty); DeepSeek-6.7B is seed-dependent: s42 82.61\% $\to$ 81.25\% (1.36\pp{} penalty), s123 74.93\% $\to$ 56.25\% (18.68\pp{} penalty). Full results appear in Appendix, Table~\ref{tab:variant_level}. The all-pass rule requires \emph{every} test in a variant to be correctly predicted; a single false negative flips the variant verdict. For variants with hundreds of tests (e.g., \texttt{astropy\_\_astropy-7336}: 357 tests, 2 false negatives $\to$ incorrect variant), even 99.4\% per-test accuracy produces a wrong variant-level prediction. \traj{} on the same 48 variants achieves 72.92\% (Qwen3, both 4B and 8B) and 75.35\% $\pm$ 5.00 (DeepSeek, 6 seeds). Within-model, Qwen3-8B \cls{} variant-level (72.92--81.25\%) brackets \traj{} (72.92\%), with the lower \cls{} seed matching exactly ($n{=}48$). \paragraph{Checkpoint selection confound.} The Qwen3-4B val-best checkpoint (per-test 83.63\%, fail recall 48.72\%) achieves lower variant-level accuracy (64.58\%) than an earlier checkpoint with lower per-test accuracy (76.92\%) but higher fail recall (79.29\%, variant-level 68.75\%). Val-based selection optimizes per-test accuracy, which biases toward predicting pass; under the all-pass rule, this bias penalizes variant-level performance. Per-test accuracy is not a reliable proxy for variant-level accuracy when aggregation rules amplify class-conditional errors. This aggregation penalty is predictable from test count: function-level variants ($\bar{T} \approx 2.3$) incur negligible penalty (per-test $\approx$ variant-level), while repo-level variants ($\bar{T} \gg 10$) incur substantial penalty. The finding connects to the oracle analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_analysis}(a)): per-test granularity concentrates its \emph{advantage} at $T \geq 2$ but also its \emph{cost} at high $T$.
tool_args.new_string: \paragraph{Aggregation penalty.} Under the all-pass rule, a single false negative flips the variant verdict. 1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We presented the first systematic comparison of three execution-free verification formulations (\cls{}, \cwm{}, \traj{}). At function level, all three achieve near-equivalent accuracy (TOST $p{=}0.007$, 5 seeds). At repository level under ${\leq}$8B LoRA fine-tuning, divergence amplifies to 19--26\pp{}, consistent across model families but model-contingent in magnitude. Per-test classification provides diagnostic granularity at comparable accuracy with 217$\times$ throughput over generation; error complementarity at function level (oracle ensemble: 90.63\%) motivates instance-level routing.
5	
6	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.} At function level, \cls{} is preferred for throughput and diagnostic signal. At repository level (${\leq}$8B), \cls{} is strongly preferred: \cwm{} falls below majority baseline (19--26\pp{} gap). Generation-based verification at repo level requires larger models or execution-trace pretraining (\S\ref{sec:threats}). When per-test diagnostics are not needed, trajectory-level scoring offers a competitive alternative with no aggregation penalty.

related_work.tex:5:Execution trace generation improves neural code reasoning~\cite{nye2021scratchpad}, with recent work extending to full output prediction~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution,liu2024codemind,liu2023codeexecutor,lee2026solidcoder}, failure analysis~\cite{abdollahi2025demystifying}, and execution-free error detection~\cite{li2024redo}. Verification formulations span trajectory-level reward~\cite{shum2025swerm,zhu2026codescaler}, process-level feedback~\cite{li2025codeprm,xu2025patchreasoner}, per-test classification~\cite{ni2023lever,chen2023codet}, and learned metrics~\cite{zhuo2024icescore,dong2024codescore,zhou2023codebertscore}. Test-time scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling,li2025sstar,chen2025vgsearch} and self-consistency~\cite{wang2023selfconsistency} demonstrate verification value. None compare formulations at matched capacity.
related_work.tex:8:Lightman et al.~\cite{lightman2023letsverify} and Uesato et al.~\cite{uesato2022solving} show process reward models (PRMs) outperform outcome reward models (ORMs) for mathematical reasoning; Math-Shepherd~\cite{wang2024mathshepherd} and OmegaPRM~\cite{luo2024omegaprm} scale process supervision via automated annotation. DreamPRM-Code~\cite{dreamprm2025code}, PRL-Coder~\cite{ye2025prlcoder}, FunPRM~\cite{zhang2026funprm}, and CodeRL+~\cite{jiang2025coderlplus} apply process-level or execution-aligned supervision to code. In the PRM/ORM framing, our \cls{} provides per-step (per-test) supervision while \traj{} provides outcome-level supervision. TOST confirms per-test and trajectory equivalence at function level ($p = 0.007$); per-test classification matches trajectory-level accuracy with additional diagnostic value. The PRM literature primarily compares supervision granularity given a fixed output format; our study additionally varies the output format itself (\cwm{} generation vs.\ \cls{} classification).

Variant-level analysis reveals this is not a coincidence: both models correctly classify all 22 unresolved variants and zero resolved variants, equivalent to an always-predict-unresolved baseline with 100\% prediction overlap. Per-test accuracy diverges sharply (Qwen3-8B 71.61\% vs.\ DeepSeek 46.28\%), but this divergence is entirely superficial: Qwen3-8B predicts pass on nearly all tests, inflating per-test accuracy on a pass-heavy dataset (72.96\% pass rate) without genuine discriminative ability. Neither 0-shot nor few-shot prompting approaches fine-tuned performance (82--84\% per-test); fine-tuning is a necessary condition for repo-level verification.
